check_description:
This check verifies that `briefing.mp4` and/or `briefing.srt` names BOTH a specific customer-concentration confirmatory-DD artefact AND a specific customer-contract-terms confirmatory-DD artefact (rather than a single artefact covering only one dimension), and names at least one specific capex / conversion-cost confirmatory artefact in the open-questions section.

The briefing must satisfy all three of: (a-i) Customer-concentration artefact: open questions name a specific concentration artefact (e.g., 'audited top-10 customer breakdown', 'customer-by-customer revenue split', or substantively equivalent). Generic 'understand customer relationships' fails. (a-ii) Customer-contract-terms artefact: open questions name a specific contract-terms artefact (e.g., 'top-3 retailer contract terms', 'retailer-contract renewal windows', 'private-label vs branded contract mix and terms', 'contract pricing pass-through clauses', or substantively equivalent). A concentration artefact alone does not satisfy this sub-criterion; the briefing must explicitly call out the contract-terms dimension as a separate confirmatory artefact. (b) Open-questions section contains at least one specific capex / conversion-cost artefact named.

Fails if: any of (a-i)/(a-ii)/(b) is generic or absent; or capex is mentioned generically without naming a specific artefact; or open questions cover capex only as a number-needs-confirming without specifying what document or figure. All three sub-criteria must pass; failure on any one fails the check.
score_0_criteria: Any of: (a-i) the customer-concentration artefact is generic ('understand customer relationships', 'review customer base') without naming a specific concentration artefact; or there is no customer-concentration open question in the briefing at all; or (a-ii) no specific customer-contract-terms artefact is named (a concentration artefact alone, e.g., 'audited top-10 customer breakdown' without a contract-terms artefact alongside, fails (a-ii)); or contract-terms surfaced only generically ('understand the contracts', 'review contract structure') without naming a specific artefact; or (b) no capex / conversion-cost question; or capex mentioned generically without naming a specific artifact; or open questions cover capex only as a number-needs-confirming without specifying what document or figure.
score_1_criteria: All three: (a-i) the open-questions section names a specific customer-CONCENTRATION artefact - examples that pass: 'audited top-10 customer breakdown', 'customer-by-customer revenue split', or substantively equivalent. Generic 'understand customer relationships' / 'review customer base' / 'top customers' fails. Anchor verbatim from Calthorpe Part 1 [00:11:51-00:12:34]: 'I'd push hard on that in confirmatory; the audited top-10 customer breakdown is the number you want.' Anchor verbatim from the internal Aurora brief: 'Customer concentration. Insider read: top 3 retailers ~70% of Aurora revenue (heavy on Foodstuffs + Woolworths NZ). Get audited top-10 in confirmatory.' AND (a-ii) the open-questions section names a specific customer-CONTRACT-TERMS artefact - examples that pass: 'top-3 retailer contract terms', 'retailer-contract renewal windows', 'private-label vs branded contract mix and terms', 'contract pricing pass-through clauses', or substantively equivalent. A single artefact (e.g., 'audited top-10 customer breakdown') that names only the concentration dimension does NOT satisfy (a-ii); the briefing must explicitly call out the contract-terms dimension as a distinct confirmatory artefact. Whether the briefing also cites the ~60-70% / ~70% figure as a finding is scoped under A-02, NOT this check; AND (b) the open-questions section names at least one specific capex / conversion-cost artefact - examples that pass: 'audited capex schedule for the colony-to-barn programme', 'signed conversion-programme contracts', 'capex-per-bird actuals vs the NZ$45-65/bird range', 'Aurora-specific capex commitment vs the NZ$11-16M estimate', or substantively equivalent. Generic 'capex needs confirming' / 'what's the capex' fails. Anchor verbatim from Calthorpe Part 2 [00:01:18]: 'The headline range I'd give you for a NZ colony-to-barn conversion is NZ$45 to NZ$65 per bird, all-in.' Anchor verbatim from Calthorpe Part 2 [00:03:32]: 'Call it NZ$11 to NZ$16 million depending on where they land in the per-bird range ... You'd want to see how it's being funded.'

check_description:
This check verifies that `briefing.mp4` and/or `briefing.srt` surfaces Aurora-specific risks with quantified $ EBITDA / % impact and source-figure citations; not generic regulatory or industry-level risks.

T4's structural cap of 3 findings + 3 open-question slots forces a subset, but the briefing must hit at least three of the four Aurora-specific quantified anchors and each named Aurora-specific risk must be source-cited.

The briefing must satisfy all of: (a) at least three of the four Aurora-specific anchors are surfaced (colony 40%/244k / NZ$3-4M EBITDA-at-risk; top-3 retailers 60-70%/~70%; FR premium 18-22% current or 18/14/12% FY26-28 trajectory on Aurora's 30% free-range mix; 12.8% margin vs 8-15%/10-12% cluster). (b) each surfaced anchor is quantified with NZ$ EBITDA impact, % revenue / volume / mix impact, or comparable specific scope. (c) every surfaced anchor cites its underlying source figure.

All three must pass. Generic listings without Aurora-specific dimensions fail. Note: the same risk dimension can be carried in either the findings or the open-questions sections; what matters is that the anchor surfaces with its quantitative figure and source citation somewhere in the briefing.
specific_file_locations:
verbatim source quotes establishing the Aurora-specific quantified-risk shortlist:

(1) colony exposure / EBITDA-at-risk:
- Halberd internal Aurora brief (`week/halberd_internal_aurora_brief_scanned.pdf`, 'Why we're looking at this'): 'Aurora's principal commercial pressure is the Phase 2 retailer-driven cage-free deadline (end-2027) against ~40% colony exposure.'
- Calthorpe Part 3 (`shared/transcript_industry_expert_part3.pdf`) [00:20:32]: '244,000 colony birds producing about 70 million eggs annualised ... Probably NZ$3-4 million EBITDA hit per year of slippage. So if they slip 12 months, the impairment is real and material on a NZ$10-11 million EBITDA business.'

(2) customer concentration:
- Halberd internal Aurora brief: 'top 3 retailers ~70% of Aurora revenue (heavy on Foodstuffs + Woolworths NZ).'
- Calthorpe Part 1 (`shared/transcript_industry_expert_part1.pdf`) [00:12:38]: 'I'd guess 60 to 70%' on top-3 retailer concentration.

(3) free-range premium compression on Aurora's 30% free-range fraction:
- Halberd internal Aurora brief: 'NZ$84.6M revenue, NZ$10.8M FY24 EBITDA (12.8% margin), 2 sites, ~610k layer hens, 40-30-30 colony / barn / free-range mix.'
- Calthorpe Part 2 (`shared/transcript_industry_expert_part2.pdf`) [00:09:38]: 'The premium they're paying for free-range over barn at the wholesale gate, in actual transaction prices in 2026, is sitting at 18 to 22%. It's not the 30%+ that gets quoted from the early Phase 1 era.'
- Calthorpe Part 3 [00:10:38]: 'FY26 averages 18% premium ... FY27 ... drops to 14%. FY28 - post-deadline ... settles at 12%.'

(4) margin vs industry range:
- Halberd internal Aurora brief: 'NZ$10.8M FY24 EBITDA (12.8% margin).'
- Calthorpe Part 1 [00:13:17]: 'EBITDA at 12.8% margin is on the high side ... Industry margin range is more like 8-15% with most operators clustering around 10-12%. Aurora at 12.8% is plausible - they've got the free-range premium pulling margin up - but I'd want to see how that's been calculated. Sometimes adjusted EBITDA on a sell-side teaser includes some one-off addbacks that wouldn't survive an audit.'

(5) sizing requirement:
- Halberd analytical standards Section 5 Risk Register Format (`shared/halberd_analytical_standards.docx`): '$ EBITDA Impact - annual EBITDA at risk (range), sourced from a quantitative anchor (interview, comp filing, or workbook)'.

check_description:
This check verifies that `briefing.srt` matches the spoken audio in `briefing.mp4` word-for-word with cue timing aligned to the narration, per the firm-wide IC convention (the audio in `briefing.mp4`; an additional submission file; not the .srt in isolation, must be used to verify verbatim text and timestamp alignment); and that `briefing.mp4` contains supporting visual content that changes through the runtime, with visuals topically aligning to the narration at major narrative beats. This is the bundled visual-quality check (formerly A-08 visual presence + A-14 visual-narration topical alignment, merged).

The submission must satisfy all of: (a) Well-formed SRT syntax: sequential indices, valid timestamps, no overlapping cues, blank-line separation, no malformed lines. (b) Subtitle text is verbatim to the spoken narration in `briefing.mp4` (no paraphrasing or re-wording). (c) Subtitle timestamps align with the audio cadence within tolerance. (d) Cue lengths are readable within standard subtitle norms. (e) visual presence with change: multiple distinct visual elements that change across the runtime. Either voiceover-with-deck or talking-head with supporting visuals is acceptable. Fails: single static title card held throughout; or talking-head with no supporting visuals at all; or generic stock imagery throughout with no specific data points referenced. (f) visual-narration topical alignment: at major narration beats (primer pillars, findings, open questions), the on-screen visual at that moment topically corresponds to what the narrator is delivering. Spoken language and visual must reference the same topic at the same moment. Failure: visual mismatched with narration topic; single static frame held through multiple distinct narrative segments; visuals out of phase across most sampled frames.

Sub-criteria (b) and (c) must be evaluated against the audio in `briefing.mp4`, not the .srt alone. If `briefing.mp4` is missing or unparseable, (b) and (c) fail. A pure talking-head video with substantive narration but no visual changes / no supporting visuals fails (e). All sub-criteria must pass; failure on any one fails the check.
score_0_criteria: Any of: (a) malformed SRT (parser errors, overlapping cues, out-of-order timestamps); or (b) subtitle text paraphrases / summarises / re-words the spoken narration in briefing.mp4 at any observable point in the audio (not verbatim); or briefing.mp4 is missing / unparseable from the submission, making (b) unverifiable; or (c) subtitle timestamps drift more than ~1 second from the audio in briefing.mp4 at multiple points; or briefing.mp4 is missing / unparseable, making (c) unverifiable; or (d) cue lengths are extreme (single-second flashes or 10+ second walls of text) at multiple points; or (e) single static title card / single frame held across the entire runtime; or talking-head with no supporting visuals at all (no slides, callouts, charts, lower-thirds intercut); or generic stock imagery throughout with no specific data points referenced; or fewer than ~6 visual changes across the runtime; or (f) visuals topically misaligned at multiple sampled moments (e.g. colony-cage chart shown while narrator discusses manure economics); or a single visual held across multiple distinct narrative segments; or visuals cycling out of phase with the narration such that >50% of sampled frames mismatch the segment they fall within.
score_1_criteria: All of: (a) well-formed SRT (parseable by standard tools - sequential indices, valid HH:MM:SS,mmm timestamps with valid ordering, no overlapping cues, blank-line separation); (b) subtitle text matches the spoken narration in briefing.mp4 word-for-word across the runtime (no paraphrasing, summarisation, or re-wording observable when cues are compared against the audio). Firm-wide convention anchor verbatim from kickoff email: 'Subtitles need to match the audio word-for-word. Hugh turns audio off in IC if subtitles are wrong.' Anchor verbatim from U007 Slack 2026-05-06: 'Hugh's IC-policy is verbatim, so don't paraphrase or summarize. Whatever the audio says, that's what the .srt says, with correct timestamps.' Anchor verbatim from IC pre-read template Section 3.4: 'Subtitles must match the audio word-for-word - spot-checked at IC. Drift between audio and subtitles is treated as a deliverable defect.'; (c) subtitle timestamps align with the spoken audio in briefing.mp4 within ~1 second across the runtime; (d) cue lengths in the 2-5 second / ~7-10 word range without extreme outliers (sub-second flashes or 10+ second walls of text); (e) visual presence with change: multiple distinct visual elements that change >=6-8 times across the runtime, with either voiceover-with-deck (slides advancing) or talking-head intercut with supporting visuals (data slides / callouts / charts). Both formats acceptable per IC pre-read template Section 3.4 verbatim: 'Single take, talking head or voiceover-with-deck'; (f) visual-narration topical alignment: at the major narration beats (primer pillars - supply chain / hen lifecycle / by-product; three findings; three open questions), the on-screen visual topically corresponds to what the narrator is delivering at that moment.

The grader receives briefing.mp4 as an additional submission file; the extracted audio (and any auto-transcribed captions surfaced in the parsed video block) should be used to verify (b) verbatim match and (c) timestamp alignment; do not rely on the .srt alone for those sub-criteria.

Cue-length tolerance band (graderside engineering defaults, not source-stated): 2-5 seconds per cue, ~7-10 words per line, two lines max. Used as a guardrail against pathological outliers (sub-second flashes or 10+ second cue walls), not fine-grained scoring.

The grader receives both briefing.mp4 (sampled frames + audio) and briefing.srt (timestamped narration) as submission files; sample the visuals at the timestamps corresponding to each major narrative beat and verify both presence and topical alignment.

check_description:
This check verifies that `briefing.mp4` and/or `briefing.srt` presents pure assessment with no recommendation, includes at least two of the three headline findings carrying an Aurora-specific anchor (with at least one of those Aurora-specific findings being sponsor-uncomfortable from the deal-defining shortlist), closes with an explicit IC-deferral phrase, presents 3 distinct findings and 3 distinct open questions — each with a numeric anchor or specific named artefact, with no paraphrase pairs across the two groups, and uses US English spelling in all written / on-screen text.

Two buried source directives must be surfaced. The MD weekly note (firm-wide archive, not in deal-team directives) carries the hard-rule balance requirement (at least one sponsor-uncomfortable headline finding) and an IC-deferral phrase rule. A separate buried Slack message from Iris in an admin channel (separate from the main deal channel; surfacing it requires pulling both Slack exports) carries the cross-group distinctness directive: findings (what we now believe) and open questions (what we still don't know) are different beasts and must not paraphrase each other across the two groups.

The briefing must satisfy all of: (a) no recommendation verbiage. (b) No thesis-pitch framing. (c) At least 2 of the 3 headline findings carry an Aurora-specific anchor (from the colony 40%/244k/NZ$3-4M EBITDA-at-risk; top-3 retailers 60-70%/~70%; FR premium 18-22% current or 18/14/12% FY26-28 trajectory; or 12.8% margin vs 8-15%/10-12% cluster shortlist), each with a quantitative anchor. At least one of those Aurora-specific anchored findings must also be sponsor-uncomfortable (per the Hugh Pemberton hard-rule balance requirement). Generic industry risks fail. (d) explicit IC-deferral phrase present. Vague hedging fails. (e) The 3 findings are distinct from each other (no within-group paraphrases). (f) Each finding carries a numeric anchor specific to Aurora or the deal context; not just a named entity. (g) The 3 open questions are distinct from each other (no within-group paraphrases). (h) Each open question is quantifiable or names a specific artefact to confirm. Generic feasibility-style questions fail.
- (i) No finding-question pair across the two groups paraphrases each other.
- (j) US English spelling across the .srt subtitle text and any on-screen text in the .mp4 (chart labels, lower-thirds, title cards). Halberd is a US private-equity firm; US English is the implicit firm-wide convention. The audio narration is harder to grade for spelling and is NOT in scope - only the written / on-screen text. Any single instance of British / Commonwealth spelling in the .srt or on-screen text fails this sub-criterion - e.g., 'realise' instead of 'realize', 'organise', 'colour', 'centre', 'programme', 'analyse', 'favour', 'behaviour', 'specialise'. Proper-noun spellings retain their canonical form (e.g., 'World Organisation for Animal Health' / WOAH, registered company names, official department names) and do not count as fails.

All sub-criteria must pass; failure on any one fails the check.
score_0_criteria: Any of: (a) explicit recommendation verbiage anywhere; or (b) thesis-pitch framing ('compelling opportunity', 'attractive asset', 'this deal works', 'why now', 'investment thesis pillars'); or (c) fewer than 2 of the 3 headline findings carry an Aurora-specific anchor from the deal-defining shortlist (e.g., only 1 finding is Aurora-specifically anchored and the other two are generic industry headwinds, or all 3 are generic); or any Aurora-specific finding lacks the required quantitative anchor (a number / % / NZ$ figure); or no Aurora-specific anchored finding is sponsor-uncomfortable (e.g., all Aurora-specific findings are framed positively, no negative-for-sponsor finding is surfaced); or (d) no explicit IC-deferral phrase ('the IC will decide' / 'this is for IC consideration' / 'the committee decides' / equivalent); vague hedging does not count; or (e) two or more findings paraphrase each other within the findings group; or (f) any finding lacks a numeric anchor (just a named entity / generic narrative); or (g) two or more open questions paraphrase each other within the questions group; or (h) any open question is generic ('is X feasible' / 'what should we think about Y') without naming a specific artifact / quantifiable target; or (i) any finding-question pair across the two groups is the same concern phrased two ways (e.g. 'customer concentration is a risk' as a finding and 'what is the customer concentration?' as an open question); or (j) any single instance of British or Commonwealth spelling in the .srt subtitle text or in any on-screen text element of the .mp4 (excluding proper nouns / registered org names; audio narration out of scope) - e.g., realise, organise, colour, centre, programme, analyse, favour, behaviour, specialise, kilometre, defence, licence (when used as a verb); one instance is enough to fail.
specific_file_locations:
no-recommendation discipline + balance + IC-deferral phrase (sub-criteria (a)-(d)):
verbatim source quotes (three layers):

(1) firm-wide no-recommendation rule:
- IC pre-read template Section 4 Hard Rules (`week/halberd_ic_preread_template.docx`) verbatim: 'No recommendations. Pre-LOI deliverables are a preliminary assessment for the IC - not an IC pitch. Decks, videos, or memos taking a recommendation position (proceed / pass / bid at X) will be rejected. Findings, risks, and open questions only. The IC decides.'
- Analytical standards Section 9 (Deal-Stage Principles and Recommendation Discipline), §9.2 Recommendation Discipline (`shared/halberd_analytical_standards.docx`) verbatim: 'No "invest" / "pass" / "continue diligence" verdict in any preliminary deliverable - pure assessment.'

(2) [buried] balance directive (Hugh Pemberton MD weekly note 2026-05-05 in `shared/halberd_md_weekly_note_archive.eml` - firm-wide MD weekly archive, not in deal-team directives) verbatim: 'The last few briefings I've sat in on read like sell-side pitches - three findings, all pointed in the same direction, no friction in the assessment. If a briefing has nothing uncomfortable in it, the team hasn't pressure-tested. I'd rather see one hard finding even if it complicates the picture. As a hard rule for pre-IC: at least one of the headline findings should be one a sponsor won't enjoy. If everything is rosy, send the team back.'

(3) [buried] IC-deferral phrase directive (Hugh Pemberton MD weekly note 2026-05-05, same source) verbatim: 'Pre-LOI briefings should surface the trade-offs and let the IC decide. Phrasing like "the IC will decide" or "this is for IC consideration" is fine and welcome - "we recommend" is not. We're coming in committed enough to be diligent; the verdict is the committee's, not the team's. If the briefing reads like the team has already made up its mind, it gets bounced.'

Hugh's note is the deepest-buried source; it sits in a firm-wide MD weekly archive (`shared/`), not in the deal team's directives; surfacing it is required to satisfy sub-criteria (c) and (d).

3+3 distinctness + numeric anchors + no cross-group paraphrase (sub-criteria (e)-(i)):
verbatim source quotes:
- IC pre-read template Section 3.4 (`week/halberd_ic_preread_template.docx`) verbatim: 'Content structure: a primer (supply chain / production economics / by-product economics), followed by the three most important findings, followed by the three most important open questions for confirmatory DD. Three plus three after the primer. No recommendation.'
- IC pre-read template Section 4 Hard Rules verbatim: 'Top three to five prioritized risks. Risk sections list the top three to five prioritized risks. More than five dilutes the IC's read; fewer than three suggests the deal team has not pressure-tested.'
- Halberd analytical standards Section 5 Risk Register Format (`shared/halberd_analytical_standards.docx`) verbatim: 'Risk Name - short specific descriptor (e.g. "Named-deadline regulatory exposure (named deadline, named trigger)"), not generic ("regulatory risk"). ... $ EBITDA Impact - annual EBITDA at risk (range), sourced from a quantitative anchor (interview, comp filing, or workbook).'

- [buried] Iris Beaumont (U007 - Halberd research analyst per `shared/slack_export_halberd/users.json`) Slack message in `#albatross-admin` (`shared/slack_export_halberd/albatross-admin/2026-05-07.json`) on 2026-05-07, verbatim: 'Quick methodology note on the Friday outputs while you're drafting - watch the finding/question duplication. Worst pattern I keep flagging on pre-IC briefings is when the team takes the same point and frames it as both a headline finding and an open question. They're meant to be different beasts: findings are what we now believe; open questions are what we still don't know and need confirmatory to resolve. If a so-called finding has a clear unknown sitting underneath it, it's an open question, not a finding - pick one and move on. The three findings and three open questions should not paraphrase each other across the two groups.'

This message lives in the admin channel (logistics + drafts coordination), not in the main `#albatross-deal` channel; surfacing it requires pulling both Slack exports.

check_description:
This check verifies that `briefing.mp4` and/or `briefing.srt` sizes the colony-deadline-slippage risk per Halberd's standards: covering Aurora's colony exposure, the end-2027 retailer deadline, and the EBITDA-at-risk per year of slippage.

The briefing must satisfy all of: (a) Aurora's colony exposure quantified. (b) The end-2027 retailer deadline is named. (c) EBITDA-at-risk per year of slippage is stated within tolerance of the source anchor (or USD equivalent with appropriate FX conversion).

All three must pass. Failure on any one fails the check.
score_0_criteria: Any one of the three missing: colony exposure not quantified (no 40% / no ~244k figure); or end-2027 deadline not named (no 2027 / no 'end-2027' / no '2028 delisting' framing); or EBITDA-at-risk per year of slippage not stated or materially outside the NZ$2-6M tolerance band (or its USD equivalent at the documented FX rate). A bare mention of '2027' without tying it to retailer-driven delisting fails the end-2027 deadline requirement; a bare mention of 'colony exposure' without 40% / 244k fails the colony-exposure requirement.
score_1_criteria: All three required: (a) Aurora's colony exposure quantified - 40% colony exposure (broker outreach: '~40% colony cage') or equivalent ~244k colony birds (Calthorpe Part 3 [00:20:32]: '244,000 colony birds'); (b) the end-2027 retailer deadline named - Calthorpe Part 3 [00:19:00] anchor: 'Foodstuffs and Woolworths NZ have made public commitments to be cage-free by end-2027'; (c) EBITDA-at-risk per year of slippage stated in the NZ$2.5-5M range (or USD equivalent at the documented FX rate). Calthorpe Part 3 [00:20:32] anchor verbatim: 'Probably NZ$3-4 million EBITDA hit per year of slippage ... on a NZ$10-11 million EBITDA business.' Tolerance band: NZ$2-6M passes; outside that range fails. Standards Section 5 verbatim: '$ EBITDA Impact - annual EBITDA at risk (range), sourced from a quantitative anchor.'

check_description:
Pairwise: which deliverable is a stronger briefing-video deliverable (`briefing.mp4` + `briefing.srt`) across five distinct dimensions?

The five dimensions:
1. narrative coherence; primer + three findings + three open questions per the firm-wide IC pre-read convention, with primer / findings / questions distinct and arranged in a coherent arc.
2. evidence anchoring; each finding and open question tied to a specific data point, source claim, or quantifiable gap rather than generic narrative or platitude. Open questions in particular must be deal-specific and quantifiable.
3. no-recommendation discipline; pure assessment with no invest / pass / continue-DD verdict, per the firm-wide rule.
4. primer pillar coverage + pacing; primer covers the three pillars (supply chain end-to-end; hen lifecycle / production economics; by-product economics) at briefing depth, paced cleanly across the runtime without rushing pillars or padding.
5. visual-narration synergy; supporting visuals in `briefing.mp4` reinforce the specific data points being narrated rather than redundantly transcribing the voice; visuals advance with narration; static title-card-only or talking-head-only deliverables lose this dimension.

Score 1 (A wins): A is stronger across the five dimensions, or strictly stronger on at least one with no regression. Score 0 (B wins): B is stronger on the same basis. Deliverables that drift outside an appropriate briefing length or contain a recommendation or omit any one of the three primer pillars at substantive depth or show only a static title card / talking-head with no supporting visuals incur an automatic loss on those respective dimensions.
score_0_criteria: Output B is stronger across the same five dimensions (or strictly stronger on at least one with no regression). Either deliverable that drifts outside an appropriate briefing length or contains a recommendation or omits any one of the three primer pillars at substantive depth or shows only a static title card / talking-head with no supporting visuals incurs an automatic loss on those respective dimensions.
score_1_criteria: Output A is stronger across the five dimensions, or strictly stronger on at least one with no regression on the others. Specifically: cleaner primer + 3 + 3 structure with primer addressing all three pillars at substantive depth; better evidence anchoring with named figures and sources for both findings and open questions (open questions are deal-specific and quantifiable); no recommendation issued; primer + findings + open questions paced cleanly across whatever runtime is chosen; visuals meaningfully reinforce specific data points across the runtime. Discriminating-figure anchors that distinguish strong from weak deliverables: NZ$455M top-down vs NZ$540M bottom-up; free-range premium 18-22% current vs 30% historical; colony-to-barn capex NZ$45-65/bird; end-2027 retailer deadline.

check_description:
Pairwise: which output is a more polished briefing-video + subtitle deliverable (`briefing.mp4` + `briefing.srt`) across five dimensions?

The five dimensions:
1. SRT syntax correctness; well-formed SRT (sequential indices, HH:MM:SS,mmm timestamps with valid ordering, no overlapping cues, blank-line separation, no malformed lines that would crash a subtitle renderer).
2. subtitle-audio alignment; subtitle text verbatim to spoken narration (per firm-wide convention) with timestamps matching audio cadence consistently across the runtime.
3. subtitle timing / readability; cue lengths readable (~2-5 seconds per cue, ~7-10 words per line, two lines max), no text too long to read in time on-screen; cue rate sustained naturally across the longer runtime.
4. audio quality; clear narration with consistent volume, no clipping, no digital artefacts, consistent voice across full runtime (no audio dropouts or volume jumps between primer / findings / open questions sections).
5. pacing across runtime; primer / findings / open questions paced cleanly: primer doesn't drag without substantive payload; findings and open questions each receive adequate runtime; transitions between sections are clean (deliberate pause, transition phrase, or visual cue rather than abrupt cut).

Score 1 (A wins): A more polished across the five dimensions: cleaner SRT syntax, more accurate subtitle-audio alignment with verbatim text sustained across full runtime, more readable cue timing, better audio quality with consistent voice, and cleaner pacing across primer / findings / open questions sections. SRT syntax errors in either output are an automatic loss on that dimension. Score 0 (B wins): B more polished on the same basis.
score_0_criteria: Output B is more polished across the same five dimensions (or strictly stronger on at least one with no regression).
score_1_criteria: Output A is more polished across the five dimensions: cleaner SRT syntax, more accurate subtitle-audio alignment with verbatim text sustained across the full runtime, more readable cue timing, better audio quality with consistent voice, and cleaner pacing across primer / findings / open questions sections. SRT syntax errors in either output are an automatic loss on that dimension.
